summary: Riding a colt down the Mount of Olives, Jesus enters Jerusalem as crowds spread cloaks and branches and shout “Hosanna!”, and He weeps over the city.
key_insight: For three years Jesus had hushed talk of His kingship. Now He planned a public claim to it, sending for a colt so that He would come exactly as Zechariah said the King would come: “Lowly, and sitting on a donkey.” His disciples, John admits, understood it only after He was glorified.
story: The day after the supper in Bethany, {Jn} Jesus went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. {Lk} Near Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, He sent two disciples into the village opposite them. They would find a colt tied, on which no one had ever sat, {Mk} and a donkey with it. {Mt} “Loose it and bring it,” He said, and if anyone asked why, they were to say, “The Lord has need of it.” {Mk}

They found the colt tied by the door outside on the street. {Mk} When its owners asked, “Why are you loosing the colt?” the disciples answered, “The Lord has need of him.” {Lk} So they let them go. {Mk} They threw their own clothes on the colt and set Jesus on it. {Lk}

All this happened, Matthew says, to fulfill the prophet’s words: “Tell the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your King is coming to you, Lowly, and sitting on a donkey, A colt, the foal of a donkey.’ ” {Mt} His disciples did not understand these things at first. Only after Jesus was glorified did they remember that these things were written about Him. {Jn}

A very great multitude spread their clothes on the road, and others spread branches cut from the trees. {Mt} From the city, a great crowd that had come to the feast took branches of palm trees and went out to meet Him. They had heard about the raising of Lazarus. {Jn}

As He came to the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen. {Lk} Those who went before and those who followed cried out, “Hosanna to the Son of David! ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the LORD!’ Hosanna in the highest!” {Mt} Some shouted, “Blessed is the kingdom of our father David” {Mk} and “The King of Israel!” {Jn}

Some of the Pharisees in the crowd called to Him, “Teacher, rebuke Your disciples.” He answered, “I tell you that if these should keep silent, the stones would immediately cry out.” {Lk} Among themselves the Pharisees said, “You see that you are accomplishing nothing. Look, the world has gone after Him!” {Jn}

As He drew near and saw the city, He wept over it: “If you had known, even you, especially in this your day, the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.” Days were coming when enemies would surround the city and level it to the ground, “because you did not know the time of your visitation.” {Lk}

When He came into Jerusalem, all the city was moved, asking, “Who is this?” The crowds answered, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.” {Mt} He went into the temple and looked around at everything. Then, as the hour was already late, He went out to Bethany with the Twelve. {Mk}
differences: Matthew mentions a donkey and her colt; Mark, Luke and John mention only the animal Jesus rode, a colt (John: “a young donkey”).
Matthew and John quote Zechariah 9:9, in different forms. John adds that the disciples understood only after Jesus was glorified.

The shouts are reported differently: “Hosanna to the Son of David!” (Matthew), “the kingdom of our father David” (Mark), “Blessed is the King” and “Peace in heaven” (Luke), “The King of Israel!” (John).
Only Luke records the Pharisees’ protest, the saying about the stones and Jesus weeping over the city. Only John mentions palm branches and the crowd who had seen Lazarus raised.
Mark says Jesus only looked around the temple that evening and returned to Bethany; Matthew and Luke move straight from the entry to the clearing of the temple.

fit.question: Matthew says the disciples brought a donkey and a colt and set Jesus “on them” (21:7). Mark, Luke and John mention only a colt. Was there one animal or two?

points.label: Mother and colt
points.text: A colt that had never been ridden would go more calmly through a shouting crowd with its mother beside it. Matthew mentions both animals; the others mention only the one Jesus rode. Naming one does not deny the other, just as with the blind men at Jericho (event 121).

points.label: “On them”
points.text: The disciples laid their clothes on both animals. In Matthew’s Greek, “set Him on them” probably refers to the clothes, spread on the colt He rode. No one needs to picture Jesus riding two animals at once.

points.label: Zechariah’s whole verse
points.text: Matthew quotes Zechariah 9:9, which speaks of “a donkey” and “a colt, the foal of a donkey” in two parallel lines, as Hebrew poetry often does. Matthew, a Jew who knew that kind of poetry, was not inventing a second animal; he reports that both were there, so the whole verse fit what happened.

fit.note: Matthew adds a detail the others leave out, as eyewitness accounts often do. Nothing here requires an error.
fit.short: The colt’s mother came too. Matthew mentions both animals; the others mention only the colt Jesus rode.

scene.label: A king on a donkey
scene.text: Horses meant war; Zechariah promised a King who would cut off the war horse and “speak peace to the nations” (Zechariah 9:10). Israel’s kings had ridden donkeys and mules in peace; David had Solomon ride his own mule to be anointed king (1 Kings 1:33). An animal never yet put to use was counted fit for a sacred purpose (compare Numbers 19:2).

scene.label: Clothes on the road
scene.text: When Jehu was proclaimed king, the officers spread their garments under him and shouted, “Jehu is king!” (2 Kings 9:13). Laying cloaks on the road was a way of saying, This is our king.

scene.label: Palms and Hosanna
scene.text: Palm branches had become a sign of national victory; when Simon Maccabeus retook Jerusalem’s fortress in 141 BC, the Jews entered with praise and palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51). “Hosanna” means “Save now,” from Psalm 118:25. Psalm 118 was part of the Hallel, the psalms sung at the great feasts, and pilgrims knew its words by heart.

scene.label: Bethphage
scene.text: A village on the Mount of Olives near Bethany; its exact site is not known. From there the road climbs over the ridge, and at the descent Jerusalem and the temple suddenly spread out below, the moment Luke says Jesus saw the city and wept.

witnesses.matthew: Shows the King fulfilling Scripture: he quotes Zechariah, names both animals and records the cry “Hosanna to the Son of David!” When the whole city asks, “Who is this?”, the crowd’s answer, a prophet from Nazareth, is true but not yet the whole truth, and the rest of the week answers the question.
witnesses.mark: Tells it with restraint and ends quietly: Jesus enters the temple, looks around at everything and leaves because the hour is late. The next morning He will act on what He saw. Mark’s crowd hails the coming kingdom “of our father David.”
witnesses.luke: Has the disciples praise God for His mighty works and cry “Peace in heaven,” an echo of the angels’ song at His birth (2:14). He alone records the Pharisees’ protest and Jesus weeping over the city that did not know “the things that make for your peace.”
witnesses.john: Links the entry to Lazarus: the crowd came out because they had heard of that sign, and the Pharisees despaired, “the world has gone after Him!” John alone mentions the palm branches and admits that the disciples understood the meaning only after Jesus was glorified.

seeing.reveals: Jesus comes as the King Zechariah promised: royal, yet lowly. He accepts the praise as His due, and in the middle of it He weeps for the city that will reject Him.
seeing.living: Within the week, Jerusalem would hand Him over to be crucified. Praise that wants a King on its own terms does not last. Welcome Him as He comes, lowly and on His way to the cross, and let His tears over Jerusalem teach you how He sees people who miss their day.
seeing.ponder: Would Jesus weep over your life as a place that does not know “the things that make for your peace”?

preaching.big_idea: The King comes lowly, receives praise, and weeps over those who miss His visit.
outline: The King weeps over the city (41–44)
preaching.watch_for: Luke frames the entry with peace. The disciples sing “Peace in heaven” (19:38), and Jesus weeps because the city does not know “the things that make for your peace” (19:42). The praise and the tears belong together.
